intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you something to remember it by and warns where people slip. Work the section exercises with a pencil, answer the recall questions before you look, and use the six aid-figure questions on any report you read.

sections.title: The Aid System
sections.big_idea: Development governance is the **system of actors, rules and money** that decides who gets resources, on what terms and for what.
in_plain_words: Think of the system in four layers. A treaty or agenda says what the world aims at, an institution holds and moves the money, an instrument decides whether it is a grant, loan, guarantee or equity, and a contract says who reports what to whom. You will mostly live in the bottom two.

Six families of actor carry nearly every development dollar, and where each one's money comes from tells you whose displeasure it must avoid. Money moves fastest, rules move slowest. Most so-called aid is debt, so grant or loan is always the first question about a figure.

diagram.caption: four layers, top first; you live in the bottom two

key_terms.meaning: Organisations, agreements, funding channels and norms through which aid is decided and delivered.
Official development assistance, the DAC's measure of qualifying aid.
A loan on softer-than-market terms, still a debt to be repaid.
Source, channel, intermediary and delivery, each link adding a cut and a rule.
Money migrants send home, bypassing the aid system entirely.

worked_example.title: Grant or loan, gross or net?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative headline: 'a country received $500 million in aid'. Of that, $400 million was concessional loans, and the country repaid $150 million on earlier loans in the same year.
steps: Grant part: 500 − 400 = 100 million.
Grant share of the headline: 100 ÷ 500 = 0.2, which is 20 percent.
Net of repayments: 500 − 150 = 350 million.
Ask the funding-chain question too: how many links lie between the donor and the district?
worked_example.answer: Only 20 percent of the headline is a gift, and net of repayments the transfer is $350 million. The first two questions are grant or loan, then gross or net.

mistakes: Treating 'aid' as a gift. Concessional loans are debts that count as aid in many ledgers.
Asking for the overhead percentage before the number of links in the funding chain.
Assuming a UN agency and a bank answer to the same body. Each family answers to different people.

recall.q: Name the four layers on slide 4.
recall.a: Treaty or agenda, institution, instrument and contract.

recall.q: Which of actors, rules and money changes fastest?
recall.a: Money, because a donor budget cut can land within months.

recall.q: Which family has no external accountability at all?
recall.a: Foundations, whose trustees answer to no electorate.

recall.q: Which is larger: ODA or domestic tax revenue?
recall.a: Domestic tax revenue is larger than all external flows combined.

recall.q: What are the first two questions about any aid figure?
recall.a: Grant or loan, and gross or net of repayments.

sections.title: A Short History
sections.big_idea: Today's system is **sediment**: each era added institutions and rules and none was repealed.
in_plain_words: Bretton Woods in 1944 created the IMF and World Bank, designed by 44 mostly Northern states, and the UN gave every state a seat. Decolonisation created new states needing capital. Cold War aid then tied allocation to strategy, and the Washington Consensus put conditions on loans.

The backlash led to the MDGs in 2000 and the SDGs in 2015. Each correction absorbed the previous critique and left the institutions in place. The system reforms its language readily and its voting shares almost never, so contradictory demands are normal.

events.what: Bretton Woods: IMF and World Bank agreed
UN founded; one nation, one vote
Cold War aid as foreign policy

diagram.caption: each era left a residue still operating

key_terms.meaning: 1944 meeting that designed the IMF and the World Bank.
1980s-90s orthodoxy of deficit cuts, privatisation and liberalisation.
Loans tied to economic reforms, reshaping economies in the Global South.
Eight goals for 2000 to 2015, aimed mainly at poor countries.
A rule or habit from an earlier era that still operates today.

worked_example.title: Match era to residue, and count the goals
worked_example.setup: Use the slide 19 table to match each residue to its era, then compare the goal counts.
steps: Weighted voting and the leadership convention come from 1944.
Aid housed in foreign ministries comes from the Cold War.
Conditionality as a normal instrument comes from adjustment.
Goals gained between MDGs and SDGs: 17 − 8 = 9.
Targets per SDG on average: 169 ÷ 17 = 9.94, about ten.
worked_example.answer: 1944, Cold War and adjustment match in that order. The SDGs have nine more goals than the MDGs and about ten targets per goal.

mistakes: Calling the system natural or inevitable. Each rule was made by someone at a moment in history.
Reading Cold War aid as proof that nothing was built. The point is that allocation was never mainly about need.
Expecting the latest agenda to have replaced earlier ones. The system accumulates.

recall.q: How many nations met at Bretton Woods?
When were the IMF and the World Bank formally established?
recall.a: December 1945.

recall.q: Who coined the term Washington Consensus and when?
recall.a: John Williamson, in 1989.

recall.q: How do the SDGs differ from the MDGs in scope?
recall.a: 17 goals and 169 targets, applying to every country, against 8 goals aimed mainly at poor countries.

recall.q: Which built-in tension does the UN and Bank pair show?
recall.a: One-nation-one-vote at the General Assembly against one-dollar-one-vote at the financial institutions.

sections.title: The UN Development System
sections.big_idea: 'The UN' is a **federation of bodies**, each with its own board, budget and rules, so always ask which one.
in_plain_words: The Secretariat, General Assembly, Security Council, funds and programmes, and specialised agencies differ in power. The General Assembly gives every state one vote but cannot compel. Funds such as UNICEF and UNDP have their own boards, and specialised agencies such as WHO have their own treaties.

Core funding is flexible and earmarked funding is tied to donors, so earmarking turns agencies into contractors. In a country the Resident Coordinator leads the team. The UN is strong on legitimacy and norms and weak on enforcement, which is the price of including everyone.

children.label: Principal bodies
items: General Assembly: every state, one vote

key_terms.meaning: Unearmarked money agencies can allocate to their own priorities.
Money tied by the donor to a country, theme or project.
Leads the UN country team; role strengthened in the 2018 reform.
Rotating body of states that approves an agency's budget and programmes.
Creating conventions and standards that states adopt.

worked_example.title: Which body, and how earmarked?
worked_example.setup: Part A: route four requests to a UN body. Part B: illustrative agency budget of 100 with 30 core, the rest earmarked.
steps: Child nutrition support: UNICEF.
Health norms and standards: WHO.
Gender equality: UN Women.
Earmarked money: 100 − 30 = 70.
Earmarked share of the budget: 70 ÷ 100 = 0.7, which is 70 percent.
worked_example.answer: UNICEF, WHO and UN Women for the three requests. In the illustrative agency 70 percent of money is earmarked, leaving 30 percent for strategy and the unglamorous.

mistakes: Saying 'the UN is doing X' without naming the body. The Secretariat, funds and specialised agencies differ.
Expecting a General Assembly resolution to bind. It creates political expectation and no legal obligation.
Approaching a country team without reading the public country framework first.

recall.q: How many votes does each state have in the General Assembly?
recall.a: One.

recall.q: Which agencies are specialised agencies with their own constitutions?
recall.a: WHO and the ILO, among others.

recall.q: Why does earmarking weaken an agency?
recall.a: It limits room for the long-term and unglamorous work and turns the agency into a contractor for the donor.

recall.q: What binds states in this system?
recall.a: Treaties that states ratify and loan agreements that borrowers sign.

recall.q: Name two strengths of the UN system.
recall.a: Any two of legitimacy, norm-setting, convening and technical depth.

sections.title: The Financial Institutions
sections.big_idea: Where the UN sets norms, the IFIs **move money with conditions attached**, and voting follows shareholding.
in_plain_words: IFIs lend at scale. The World Bank Group has five arms: IBRD for middle-income governments, IDA for the poorest, IFC for companies, MIGA for guarantees and ICSID for disputes. The IMF lends in balance-of-payments crises, and its approval signals to other creditors.

Votes follow capital, so the richest nations decide, and an unwritten convention fills the top jobs. Conditionality is where finance becomes politics. New banks such as AIIB and NDB add competition, but reform stalls because those who hold votes must agree to lose them.

key_terms.meaning: World Bank arms for middle-income governments / the poorest.
Lender of last resort in balance-of-payments crises.
Policy terms a borrower must meet to receive or keep a loan.
The IMF's assessment as a signal to other creditors.
An IMF member's share, which sets its votes.

worked_example.title: Match clients and conditions
worked_example.setup: Match four clients to World Bank arms, then sort four conditions into types from slide 36. IDA is replenished every three years.
steps: A creditworthy middle-income government: IBRD.
A low-income government needing grants and cheap credit: IDA.
A private company: IFC. An investor wanting political-risk cover: MIGA.
Deficit target: macroeconomic. Privatisation: structural. Procurement rule: governance. Protected health spending: social floor.
Over nine years there are 9 ÷ 3 = 3 IDA replenishment rounds.
worked_example.answer: IBRD, IDA, IFC and MIGA match in that order, and the conditions sort as macroeconomic, structural, governance and social floor, with three replenishments in nine years.

mistakes: Treating the IMF as a development bank. It lends in crisis and does not fund projects.
Expecting the leadership convention to be repealed. It is unwritten, so it can only be outvoted.
Assuming conditionality is only harmful or only helpful. Both defences hold at once.

recall.q: What does IDA do and how often is it replenished?
recall.a: Grants and cheap credit to the poorest, replenished by donor pledges every three years.

recall.q: Which two institutions did Bretton Woods create?
recall.a: The IMF and the World Bank.

recall.q: What is the NDB's difference from Bretton Woods?
recall.a: It has equal founding shareholding for BRICS members.

recall.q: Why is reform of voting shares slow?
recall.a: Those who hold the votes must vote to dilute their own power.

recall.q: What is the seal of approval effect?
recall.a: A country off track with the IMF finds bilateral and market finance harder to obtain.

sections.title: Bilateral & Multilateral Aid
sections.big_idea: Most aid statistics describe **DAC members only**, and the DAC's definition of ODA decides what the totals show.
in_plain_words: Bilateral aid gives the donor control and visibility, and multilateral aid pools money and cuts transaction costs for recipients. The OECD-DAC defines ODA, collects statistics and reviews members, and it excludes China, India and Gulf donors.

ODA must be official, concessional and developmental. Only the grant element of a loan counts. Some items count without leaving the donor country, and tied aid raises costs. The 0.7 percent of GNI target has mostly gone unmet. Six questions resolve most contradictions between aid figures.

diagram.note: the 1970 UN target is 0.7% of GNI; most donors have never reached it

key_terms.meaning: Club of traditional donors that defines and counts ODA.
The discount a loan carries versus a commercial loan.
Aid that must be spent on goods and services from the donor country.
Promised against actually paid.
UN General Assembly goal of 0.7% of GNI as ODA, set in 1970.

worked_example.title: Test a donor against the target
worked_example.setup: Illustrative donor with gross national income of $1,000 billion that gives $3 billion of ODA, of which a $100 million loan carries a 40% grant element.
steps: The target amount: 1,000 × 0.007 = 7 billion.
Actual share: 3 ÷ 1,000 = 0.003, which is 0.3 percent.
Shortfall against the target: 7 − 3 = 4 billion.
A $100 million loan at a 40% grant element counts as 100 × 0.4 = 40 million of ODA under grant-equivalent rules.
worked_example.answer: The donor gives 0.3 percent of GNI against 0.7, a $4 billion shortfall, and the loan adds only $40 million of aid, with the other $60 million left as debt.

mistakes: Reading 'global aid fell' as a statement about all donors. It is usually DAC members only.
Counting a whole loan as aid. Only the grant equivalent counts.
Trusting 'aid rose' without checking in-donor costs such as first-year refugee costs.

recall.q: Why do recipients prefer multilateral channels?
recall.a: Lower transaction costs: one relationship instead of thirty bilateral reporting regimes.

recall.q: What three tests define ODA?
recall.a: Official, concessional and developmental in purpose.

recall.q: When was the 0.7 percent target set?
recall.a: 1970, by the UN General Assembly.

recall.q: Since when has the DAC discouraged tied aid?
Name two of the six aid-data questions.
recall.a: Any two of grant or loan, gross or net, committed or disbursed, year and prices, in-donor costs, bilateral or multilateral.

sections.title: The SDGs & 2030 Agenda
sections.big_idea: The SDGs are a **shared map and an accountability language**, with no funding attached and goals that pull on each other.
in_plain_words: Agenda 2030 has 17 goals and 169 targets, adopted in September 2015. Financing was agreed separately at Addis in July 2015. The SDGs are universal, so every country reports through voluntary reviews, and leave no one behind means reaching the poorest first.

Disaggregated data is missing for many indicators, so averages can hide the abandoned. The goals interact: educating girls helps health, gender and income but can strain consumption and climate. South Asia shows gains alongside persistent gaps in nutrition, sanitation and air quality.

diagram.caption: a chain across goals, as on slide 53

key_terms.meaning: Transforming Our World, adopted by all UN member states in 2015.
Pledge to reach the poorest and most marginalised first.
Voluntary National Review, a government's self-reported progress.
Data split by income, sex, disability, location or group.
A grade of methodological maturity for an SDG indicator.

worked_example.title: How an average hides the abandoned
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 90% of a country's people have 75% coverage of a service and the poorest 10% have 20%. Then count the goals.
steps: Weighted contribution of the majority: 0.9 × 75 = 67.5.
Contribution of the poorest tenth: 0.1 × 20 = 2.
National average: 67.5 + 2 = 69.5 percent.
Goals added since the MDGs: 17 − 8 = 9.
worked_example.answer: The national average of 69.5 percent hides coverage of only 20 percent for the poorest tenth, which is why disaggregated data matters. The SDGs have nine more goals than the MDGs.

mistakes: Picking goals like a menu. The framework treats the 17 as a system.
Reading a VNR as verified. It is the government reporting on itself, so look for shadow reports.
Replacing an unavailable indicator with another one without saying so.

recall.q: How many goals and targets does Agenda 2030 have?
recall.a: 17 goals and 169 targets.

recall.q: Where was SDG financing agreed and when?
recall.a: At Addis Ababa, in July 2015.

recall.q: What is the biggest shift from the MDGs?
recall.a: Universality: the SDGs apply to every country.

recall.q: What does leave no one behind require?
recall.a: Data disaggregated by income, sex, disability, location and group.

recall.q: What is NITI Aayog's SDG India Index?
recall.a: A self-assessment that scores states and union territories on indicators India selected.

sections.title: Financing for Development
sections.big_idea: No single source funds the SDGs. **Domestic tax is the largest**, and aid is one slice of a portfolio.
in_plain_words: Monterrey in 2002, Doha in 2008 and Addis Ababa in 2015 moved the debate from aid alone to all sources, with domestic resource mobilisation first. Taxing fairly also builds accountability, because a government funded by taxpayers answers to them.

Money leaks out through profit shifting, mis-invoicing, evasion and tax incentives. Debt can finance growth, but shocks and diverse private creditors turn it into distress. Blended finance promises a multiplier and delivers modest ratios. For your project, ask which source sustains it after you leave.

key_terms.meaning: Domestic resource mobilisation: building capacity to tax fairly.
Profit shifting, mis-invoicing and evasion moving money to tax havens.
Whether debt can be serviced without cutting essential services.
Public or philanthropic money used to reduce risk and attract private capital.
Aid used for recurrent costs that stops when the funding ends.

worked_example.title: Aid against a few points of tax
worked_example.setup: Illustrative country with GDP of $100 billion. Aid receipts are 2% of GDP. A reform raises tax by 3 points of GDP. A blended deal puts $10 million of public money beside $20 million of private.
steps: Aid received: 100 × 0.02 = 2 billion.
Extra tax from the reform: 100 × 0.03 = 3 billion.
Private dollars per public dollar in the blended deal: 20 ÷ 10 = 2.
The deck calls realised ratios typically modest.
worked_example.answer: The reform raises $3 billion against $2 billion of aid, without conditions or repayment. The blended deal draws two private dollars per public dollar.

mistakes: Funding recurrent salaries with aid, which creates a cliff when the project ends.
Quoting an illicit flows total without its method. Estimates vary widely.
Treating debt distress as only imprudence. Shocks arrive on exposed balance sheets, and creditors extended the credit.

recall.q: What did the Addis Ababa Action Agenda put first?
recall.a: Domestic resource mobilisation.

recall.q: Which conference took place in 2002?
recall.a: Monterrey.

recall.q: Why is debt restructuring slower than before?
recall.a: Creditors are now diverse and private, and each gains by holding out.

recall.q: What two questions should you ask of a blended finance deal?
recall.a: Which party bears the first loss, and what happens if the project fails.

recall.q: Why is tax incentives the most tractable leak?
recall.a: They are legal, and a government can repeal its own exemptions.

sections.title: New & Shifting Actors
sections.big_idea: More money and more choice, but also **fragmented rules and new accountability gaps**.
in_plain_words: Foundations, emerging-economy donors, corporations, global funds and INGOs now sit beside states and the UN. Large foundations answer to their trustees, South–South providers to their own governments and corporations to shareholders. Non-DAC providers do not report to the DAC, so official statistics miss their flows.

China's Belt and Road offers speed and few conditions, with opacity as the best-documented concern. Companies bring scale but also PPP liabilities that sit off budget until called. A weak finance ministry facing thirty uncoordinated funders gains little from choice.

children.label: Emerging-economy donors
items: China and the Belt and Road

key_terms.meaning: Development cooperation between developing countries as partners.
Belt and Road Initiative, China's infrastructure lending programme.
A donor outside the OECD-DAC, reporting by its own rules.
Public-private partnership, shared risk with possible contingent liabilities.
A system with several centres of money and influence.

worked_example.title: Missing flows and a called guarantee
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: DAC data shows $80 million of external finance to a country, and researchers estimate $20 million from non-DAC providers. Separately, a state gave a $200 million PPP guarantee, and 25% is called.
steps: Total external finance: 80 + 20 = 100 million.
DAC-only data understates by 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2, which is 20 percent.
Guarantee called: 200 × 0.25 = 50 million.
Until called the guarantee is off budget. Once called, it is debt.
worked_example.answer: DAC-only data misses 20 percent of external finance. The called guarantee turns $50 million of off-budget promise into debt.

mistakes: Reading South–South framing as proof of selflessness, or as proof of the opposite. Check the actual terms.
Assuming the Belt and Road is a deliberate debt trap. The evidence for asset seizure is weak, and opacity is the clearer problem.
Treating 'more choice' as a universal benefit. It depends on state capacity.

recall.q: Who are large foundations accountable to?
recall.a: Their own trustees.

recall.q: Why do official aid statistics miss non-DAC flows?
recall.a: Those providers do not use the ODA definition or report to the DAC.

recall.q: What is the underappreciated risk in PPPs?
recall.a: Guarantees sit off-budget until called, then they become debt.

recall.q: Under which Act is CSR a statutory obligation in India?
recall.a: The Companies Act.

recall.q: What does the slide 72 table say multipolarity costs?
recall.a: More reporting regimes, harder national coordination, weaker collective standards and less scrutiny of terms.

sections.title: Aid Effectiveness & Localisation
sections.big_idea: Aid quality matters as much as quantity, and **sharing power is harder than signing declarations**.
in_plain_words: Fragmented projects, parallel systems and volatile disbursement overwhelm recipient ministries. The Paris Declaration of 2005 set five principles: ownership, alignment, harmonisation, results and mutual accountability. Accra deepened ownership, and Busan widened the group but made commitments voluntary for new donors.

Localisation shifts money, decisions, leadership and risk to local organisations, and the Grand Bargain of 2016 committed donors to direct funding. Decolonising aid asks deeper questions about whose knowledge counts. Obstacles hold because incentives reward whoever already holds the money.

diagram.caption: from a small club to everyone who matters

key_terms.meaning: Countries lead their own development plans.
Donors back national plans and use country systems.
Donors coordinate to reduce duplication.
Shifting funding and leadership to local and national organisations.
2016 commitments to make aid more efficient and more direct to local responders.

worked_example.title: The reporting burden and the capacity test
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a health ministry deals with 30 donors, each needing 4 reports a year. Harmonisation would move them to one shared format.
steps: Reports with separate formats: 30 × 4 = 120 a year.
Reports in one shared format per donor: 30 × 1 = 30.
Time saved on form-filling: 120 − 30 = 90 reports.
Capacity test: what counts as sufficient capacity, who assesses it and on what timetable?
worked_example.answer: Harmonisation would cut 120 reports to 30, saving 90. The capacity test shows whether 'capacity' is a real obstacle or a way to defer transfer.

mistakes: Treating direct funding percentages as the measure of localisation. Money with the same conditions transfers no decision-making.
Assuming Busan strengthened the regime. It widened it, and made commitments voluntary for new providers.
Accepting 'capacity' as a reason to delay power-sharing without asking who assesses it.

recall.q: What are the five Paris principles?
recall.a: Ownership, alignment, harmonisation, results and mutual accountability.

recall.q: Which Paris principle is hardest?
recall.a: Alignment, because donors must accept audit risk in another state's systems.

recall.q: When was the Grand Bargain and what did it commit?
recall.a: 2016, to channel more funding as directly as possible to local responders.

recall.q: What is the difference between localisation and decolonising aid?
recall.a: Localisation concerns the flow of funds and authority; decolonising questions whose knowledge counts and who is expert.

recall.q: What is the sharpest criticism of localisation?
recall.a: Risk is pushed down to the local partner and left unshared.

sections.title: Critiques & Power
sections.big_idea: Aid has saved lives and distorted incentives. Hold both, and ask **who decides and who answers to whom**.
in_plain_words: Three positions say aid works, harms or is marginal, and they describe different things: interventions, incentives and aggregate growth. Dependency, Dead Aid, paternalism and conditionality each raise a question about accountability and sovereignty. The cash transfer evidence is a rebuke to assumed preferences.

Power also runs through measurement: which outcomes count, whose indicators, which language. Accountability is wired upward to donors and downward accountability is thin. The balanced stance is specific: this instrument, in this country, with these terms, is or is not doing what it claims.

key_terms.meaning: Aid weakening accountability and local markets over time.
Moyo's 2009 critique of government-to-government aid to Africa.
Outsiders deciding what people need without real partnership.
Who sets policy when loan conditions require it.
Answering to the communities served, through feedback and redress.

worked_example.title: When does the dependency argument bite?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: Country A has a budget of 100 with 5 from aid. Country B has a budget of 100 with 60 from aid. The deck says the accountability argument is weak for a small aid share and strong where aid funds most spending.
steps: Country A aid share: 5 ÷ 100 = 0.05, which is 5 percent.
Country B aid share: 60 ÷ 100 = 0.6, which is 60 percent.
A is closer to the weak case, and B to the strong case.
Next, match claims to positions: saved lives at scale is 'aid works'; weakened accountability is 'aid harms'.
worked_example.answer: Country A's aid share is 5 percent and B's is 60 percent, so the dependency argument applies to B far more than to A.

mistakes: Citing Dead Aid against health or humanitarian aid. The book targeted government-to-government aid in Africa.
Running a consultation that cannot change the programme. Participants see it as legitimation.
Treating the aid debate as two sides to pick. Aid works where the outcome is technical and badly where it substitutes for a political settlement.

recall.q: Name the three positions in the 'does aid work' debate.
recall.a: Aid works, aid harms and aid is marginal.

recall.q: Why is downward accountability weaker?
recall.a: It has no legal instrument behind it, so it rests on goodwill.

recall.q: What does the cash transfer evidence show about preferences?
recall.a: People spend money broadly as they said they would, which contradicts what paternalist design assumed.

recall.q: Where does the slide say the dependency argument is strong?
recall.a: Where aid funds a majority of public spending.

recall.q: What stance does the balanced view recommend?
recall.a: Specific judgement: this instrument, in this country, with these terms.

sections.title: India in the System
sections.big_idea: India is **both recipient and provider**, and its framing and its record are separate evidence.
in_plain_words: India moved from one of the largest aid recipients to a provider of cooperation, while still borrowing from the World Bank and ADB. The 1991 IMF programme shapes how conditionality is remembered. Cooperation runs through the MEA and its Development Partnership Administration, mostly as concessional lines of credit.

India frames this as South–South partnership with no policy conditionality, yet lines of credit often specify Indian sourcing, which is tied aid by the standard definition. Its 2023 G20 presidency won a permanent seat for the African Union and pushed MDB reform. Reform demands meet the usual structural fact.

key_terms.meaning: Development Partnership Administration within the MEA.
Concessional loan for partner-country projects, administered via Exim Bank.
Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation training programme.
Aid whose contracts must source from the provider country.
India's summits and advocacy for fairer representation.

worked_example.title: Apply the aid-figure questions to India
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: India reports $1,000 million of development cooperation, of which $900 million is lines of credit (the dominant instrument).
steps: Grants and other non-loan items: 1,000 − 900 = 100 million.
Grant share: 100 ÷ 1,000 = 0.1, which is 10 percent.
Question 1: grant or loan? Mostly loans, so mostly debt.
Question 2: tied? If contracts specify Indian sourcing, it is tied aid by the standard definition.
worked_example.answer: In this illustration only 10 percent is grant, and the lines of credit are debt, possibly tied. The same tests apply to India as to DAC donors.

mistakes: Holding India's 'partnership' framing as proof of selfless aid. All providers serve strategic and commercial interests.
Forgetting India still borrows from the World Bank and ADB.
Judging the G20 presidency by what it proposed. The firm outcome was the African Union's admission.

recall.q: Which Indian bodies run development cooperation?
recall.a: The Ministry of External Affairs and its Development Partnership Administration.

recall.q: What is India's dominant instrument by value?
recall.a: Lines of credit, which are concessional loans.

recall.q: Why does sourcing matter?
recall.a: Contracts that specify Indian sourcing are tied aid by the standard definition.

recall.q: What was the concrete outcome of the 2023 G20?
recall.a: The African Union became a permanent member.

recall.q: Which three questions does the final slide recommend for any development figure?
recall.a: Who counted it, under whose definition, and whether it is a gift or a loan.

notes.2: This agenda shows the course as **eleven sections that move from a map of the system to your own position in it**. Sections 1 to 5 describe actors and money, 6 and 7 the goals and their financing, 8 to 10 the shifts and critiques, and 11 turns to India. Keep section 1 in mind throughout.
notes.4: Remember the four layers: **treaty, institution, instrument, contract**. Each answers a different question, from what the world aims at to who reports what to whom. You will seldom negotiate the top two layers and you will live inside the bottom two, so learn where your funder's rules came from.
notes.5: Hold three words together: **actors, rules and money**. Money moves fastest, because a donor budget cut lands within months, while rules move slowest and matter longest. The definitions of aid agreed in the 1960s still shape today's totals. When something changes in your work, ask which of the three moved.
notes.6: Learn the six families by name, then read the last two columns of the second table together. The slide's point is that **where an actor's money comes from predicts its behaviour** better than its mandate does. The foundation row has no external accountability at all, which is the substance of the critique of big philanthropy.
notes.7: Follow the funding chain from source to delivery and notice that **each link takes a cut, adds a rule and loses some intent**. Audit and evaluation are real costs, so a long chain is not waste by definition. The slide's practical tip: ask for the number of links before the overhead percentage.
notes.8: Treat 'aid' as two different things: **grants, which are never repaid, and loans, which are**. A concessional loan counts as ODA when its grant element is high enough. So the first question about any aid figure is grant or loan, and the second is gross or net of repayments. Many headline totals are gross.
notes.9: Get the ordering right and avoid false precision: **domestic tax revenue exceeds all external flows combined**, remittances exceed ODA, and ODA runs to hundreds of billions a year. The slide calls aid catalytic and never the main event. Remittances bypass the system, with no conditionality and no intermediary.
notes.10: Use this slide to explain **why the course is practical**. Your funder's audit rules become yours, SDG targets reach your logframe, power is unequal and new funders change what is possible. The closing paragraph gives a test: a demand rooted in a donor's legislation will not move, while one from a template usually will.
notes.12: Bretton Woods in 1944 produced the IMF and the World Bank, **designed by 44 mostly Northern states** while much of Africa and Asia was still colonised. The founding membership is visible today in voting shares and the leadership convention, which is why reform debates keep returning to 1944. The institutions were formally established in December 1945.
notes.13: Independence created sovereign states that needed capital, expertise, a voice and fair trade, and the system offered loans with terms set elsewhere. The key mismatch sits in the third row: an **equal vote at the UN but weighted votes at the Bank**. That fact underlies sixty years of reform demands.
notes.14: Remember the tension built into the system from 1945: the General Assembly is **one-nation-one-vote**, while the financial institutions are one-dollar-one-vote. Two different ideas of fairness operate side by side, and your work will meet both. The UN also grew a large family of agencies for health, children, food, labour and development.
notes.15: Cold War aid shows that **strategic interest has always shaped where the money goes**. Read the table as habits that outlived the Soviet Union: allocation that follows strategy, support for friendly governments, and aid housed in foreign ministries. The slide adds that Cold War aid did build things, but allocation was never mainly about need.
notes.16: The Washington Consensus meant loans with conditions: cut deficits, privatise, deregulate, open to trade. The critique that stuck concerned **sequencing and social cost**. Williamson coined the term in 1989 and later objected to its stretch into market fundamentalism. UNICEF's Adjustment with a Human Face made the critique from inside the system.
notes.17: Read the timeline as a pattern: each correction **absorbed the previous critique and left the institutions in place**. The Bank and the Fund turned to poverty and were not displaced. The slide's lesson is that the system reforms its language and indicators readily, and its voting shares almost never.
notes.18: The chart compares goal counts: eight MDGs from 2000 to 2015 and 17 SDGs with 169 targets from 2015 to 2030. The deeper change is in who the goals cover. The MDGs aimed mainly at poor countries, and the **SDGs apply to every nation, rich and poor**.
notes.19: Think of the system as **sediment**: each era left a residue that was never repealed, from weighted voting in 1944 to indicator politics today. The practical consequence is that contradictory demands are normal. Country ownership and donor conditionality are both live rules, written in different decades.
notes.21: Ask **which UN body** whenever someone says 'the UN'. The General Assembly, Security Council, Secretariat, funds and programmes, and specialised agencies each have different powers. WHO and ILO are specialised agencies with their own constitutions, while UNICEF and UNDP are funds and programmes. The answer decides the rules, the reporting and who can commit.
notes.22: Use the second table as a **routing guide**: governance goes to UNDP, children to UNICEF, health to WHO, gender to UN Women, food to FAO, WFP and IFAD, and refugees to UNHCR. Mandates overlap heavily, with nutrition as the example, and agencies compete for the same earmarked money. That competition explains why coordination reform stalls.
notes.23: Two kinds of body steer the system. The General Assembly gives every state one vote but **cannot compel**, and each agency's executive board approves its own budget. The slide's summary is that power is diffuse. Binding instruments are treaties that states ratify and loan agreements that borrowers sign. Everything else works by expectation and money.
notes.24: Core funding is flexible and multi-year, and earmarked funding is tied to a donor's choice. The table's overhead row explains a chronic complaint: **earmarked money recovers overheads at capped, often sub-cost rates**, so agencies subsidise projects from a shrinking core. Core pays for norm-setting and the uncomfortable conversations with governments.
notes.25: The chart is illustrative, so use it for direction only. As earmarking grows, agencies lose room for **the unglamorous, the long-term and the politically awkward**. Donors gain control and agencies lose strategy. When you read an agency's funding, ask how much of it is core.
notes.26: Know the chain in a country: the Resident Coordinator leads the UN country team, a framework is agreed with the government, agencies deliver within their mandates, and partners work on the ground. **Read the public country framework before any approach**, since it shows what the UN has committed to for several years. The 2018 reform strengthened the RC role.
notes.27: The UN's strengths are **legitimacy, norm-setting, convening and technical depth**. The norm-setting record is the most durable and the least visible: conventions on children, women and disability are cited in domestic litigation. Neutrality is relative, since agencies depend on donor funding and host-government consent.
notes.28: The limits are the price of the strengths. Including every state makes the system slow and consensus-bound, and it cannot compel a member without consent. Expect underfunded cores, four agencies with four reporting formats, and commitments with no penalty for breach. The slide calls the trade-off **structural**, which is why reform proposals that assume it away have gone nowhere.
notes.30: IFIs lend at scale and **attach conditions**, so they hold influence that UN agencies lack. The last row explains the scale: the World Bank borrows on capital markets against its shareholders' backing, so one dollar of paid-in capital supports many dollars of lending. Its AAA rating makes cheap lending possible and limits how much risk it takes.
notes.31: Learn the five arms by what each does and who repays: IBRD lends near market terms to middle-income governments, IDA gives grants and cheap credit to the poorest, IFC invests in firms, MIGA gives political-risk guarantees and ICSID settles disputes. **IDA is replenished every three years** by donor pledges, so it is the most exposed to donor politics.
notes.32: The IMF lends in a balance-of-payments crisis in exchange for policy reforms, and does not fund development projects. Its influence exceeds its lending because of the **seal-of-approval effect**: a country off track with the Fund finds other finance harder to get. Whether softer conditions changed outcomes is still argued.
notes.33: The ADB (1966), the NDB (2015) and the AIIB (2016) show that the system is **no longer monopolised**. The NDB's equal founding shares deliberately contrast with Bretton Woods. The practical effect so far is more competition for infrastructure lending and pressure on older institutions over speed and safeguards.
notes.34: At the Bank and the Fund, **votes follow money**: the more capital, the more votes. The chart is illustrative, so use it for the idea only. The slide notes that the US has historically held enough of a share to veto major changes alone. Compare this with the one-nation-one-vote General Assembly.
notes.35: The leadership convention is a pact written in no statute: an American at the World Bank and a European at the IMF. Because it is unwritten it cannot be repealed, only outvoted, so **every reform push targets voting shares**. Both institutions opened their selection processes and got the same outcome, which shows shareholding decides.
notes.36: Conditionality is **where finance becomes politics**. The table sorts conditions into macroeconomic, structural, governance and social floors, each contested for a different reason. Both defences hold at once: lenders may set terms, and unelected outsiders may override an electorate. The useful question is narrower: which conditions, decided by whom, on what evidence.
notes.37: List the reform demands next to their obstacles: re-weighting votes, opening leadership, softer lending and lighter conditionality. The common obstacle is that **those who hold the votes must vote to lose them**. Recent momentum comes from stretching existing capital further, which needs no redistribution of votes.
notes.39: Bilateral aid keeps control and visibility with the donor, and multilateral aid pools money and spreads the burden. Recipients prefer multilateral channels for **transaction cost** alone, since thirty bilateral donors mean thirty reporting regimes. The compromise donors use is earmarked funding through a multilateral, which gives them both.
notes.40: When you read global aid totals, they usually mean the **OECD-DAC members' ODA**. The DAC defines what counts, collects statistics and reviews members, and it does not bind anyone to give more. China, India and Gulf donors sit outside it, so a statement that global aid fell is a statement about DAC members only.
notes.41: ODA must be official, concessional and developmental, and go to an eligible recipient. The wrinkle is that some items count without leaving the donor country, such as first-year in-donor refugee costs. That makes 'aid rose' sometimes compatible with **less money reaching any developing country**. Check the composition before you read a trend.
notes.42: The 0.7 percent of GNI target was set by the UN General Assembly in 1970, and most donors have never met it. The donor bars in the chart are illustrative, but the line is real. Use the target as the **yardstick for any donor's generosity**: only a handful meet it consistently.
notes.43: A loan's grant element is its discount against a commercial loan, and **only that gift part is aid** under modern rules. The grant element depends on the assumed discount rate, and the DAC changed the method in 2018, which changed totals without changing any money. For the borrower, the debt service schedule is the number that matters.
notes.44: Tied aid must be spent on donor-country goods and firms, which raises costs and weakens ownership. The DAC has discouraged it since 2001, but tying by other means, such as donor-staffed technical assistance, is harder to see. Treat any **cost premium figure as contested** and check its source.
notes.45: The chart is illustrative, so use it for the idea that aid is unevenly distributed. The slide's point is that allocation follows need and interest: geopolitics, history and security all tilt the map. Ask of any donor's regional split which of those forces explains it.
notes.46: Keep this as a **six-question checklist** for every aid figure: grant or loan, gross or net, committed or disbursed, which year and prices, in-donor costs, and bilateral or multilateral. The slide says these resolve most apparent contradictions between two published figures. When you publish a figure, answer them in a footnote.
notes.48: Agenda 2030 has 17 goals and 169 targets, adopted in September 2015, and its weakness sits in the last row: **financing is not attached** and was agreed separately at Addis in July 2015. Read the SDGs as a shared map and an accountability language. They tell you what was agreed, and the funding is a separate question.
notes.49: The biggest shift from the MDGs is **universality**: the SDGs ask every country to act, including rich ones. They were negotiated by all states, where the MDGs were drafted by experts. The trade-off is that 169 targets do not set priorities, so national plans have to.
notes.50: 'Leave no one behind' responds to an MDG lesson: a **national target can be met while the poorest stagnate**. It requires knowing who they are, which needs data disaggregated by income, sex, disability, location and group. That data is missing for a large share of indicators in most countries.
notes.51: Universality means rich countries report too, through Voluntary National Reviews. The slide's caution is that a VNR is the government **reporting on itself**, with no verification and no consequence for omission. Look for civil-society shadow reports alongside it, since they are often the more useful document.
notes.52: Hundreds of indicators are needed for 169 targets, and for many the data is missing, out of date or not disaggregated. The chart is illustrative. Indicators are graded by methodological maturity, so **check the tier before citing one**, and say so when an indicator is unavailable instead of substituting another.
notes.53: The goals are a system and a menu does not describe them. The chain shows how educating girls links to health, gender and income, and can then strain consumption and climate goals. The table shows where each goal reinforces or conflicts. **Name the trade-off in your own design** so it stays explicit.
notes.54: South Asia holds a large share of the world's poor, so SDG 1 is central, with gains in health and poverty and persistent gaps in nutrition, gender, sanitation and air quality. NITI Aayog's SDG India Index is a **self-assessment** on indicators India chose. Check whether a state figure comes from a survey or from administrative reporting.
notes.56: Meeting the SDGs takes trillions, far beyond what aid can supply. The chart is illustrative and carries no dollar figure, but its message is that the **gap between need and finance is large and persistent**. Financing for development is the global conversation about where that money will come from.
notes.57: Trace the sequence: Monterrey 2002, Doha 2008, Addis Ababa 2015. Addis moved the emphasis from aid alone to all sources and **put domestic resource mobilisation first**. Its unfinished business is tax: developing countries asked for an intergovernmental tax body at the UN and did not get one.
notes.58: A country's own tax revenue is the largest and most sustainable source. A few points of GDP in extra tax can dwarf total aid receipts, **without conditions or repayment**. The accountability argument is the one most often skipped: a government funded by taxpayers answers to them in a way an aid-funded one does not.
notes.59: Illicit flows and tax avoidance can exceed the aid coming in. Note the last row: **tax incentives are legal**, so they sit outside illicit-flow headlines yet may be the largest and most tractable item, since a government can repeal its own exemptions. Estimates vary widely by method, so cite the method alongside any total.
notes.60: Debt sustainability asks whether a country can pay without cutting essential services. Warning signs include debt service above health spending and short maturities in foreign currency. The structural change is that **creditors are now diverse and private**, which is why restructurings take years: each creditor gains by holding out.
notes.61: Follow the loop: borrow, shock, repayments rise as revenue falls, then a choice between servicing debt and funding services. Three of the four steps are outside the borrower's control. The slide's closing point: **someone extended the credit**, and creditor behaviour is scrutinised far less than borrower behaviour.
notes.62: Blended finance uses public money to cut risk so private capital comes in. The caution is in the table: realised ratios are typically modest, flows concentrate in middle-income markets and the public side often absorbs the downside. Ask **who bears the first loss** and what happens if the project fails.
notes.63: Development finance is a **portfolio**: domestic tax is largest, remittances are very large, ODA is modest and catalytic, private investment is selective, and borrowing is flexible. Aid used for recurrent salaries creates a cliff. Ask which source can sustain the activity after your project ends, and say so in the proposal.
notes.65: The field now includes foundations, emerging-economy donors, corporations and global funds, each answerable to different bodies. Plurality gives a recipient bargaining power, and it also **fragments the rules**, because no single aid-effectiveness regime has been signed by all significant financiers.
notes.66: Large foundations such as Gates fund at a scale that rivals mid-sized donor governments, especially in global health. They work through grant scale, funding evidence, board seats and advocacy. The accountability question is **structural**: the trustees they appoint answer to no electorate, and no member state can outvote them.
notes.67: South–South cooperation is framed as solidarity between equals, with **no policy conditionality**, which recipients say is a real difference. It is also a positioning strategy in a competitive market. You can hold both readings. Ask what the terms of a given agreement are, since the sincerity of the framing cannot be checked.
notes.68: Belt and Road loans bring speed, scale and few policy conditions, and they build infrastructure others stopped funding. The 'debt trap' framing is contested, since evidence of a strategy to seize assets is weak. The clearer problem is **opacity**: where terms are unpublished, citizens and other creditors cannot assess the obligation.
notes.69: Non-DAC providers do not use the ODA definition or report to the DAC, so official statistics miss a fast-growing slice of flows. Researchers' contract-level estimates are the best available and are contested, so **cite them as estimates**. Any 'total external finance' figure built on DAC data alone understates it.
notes.70: Business enters as financier, implementer, PPP partner and CSR funder. The underappreciated item is **PPP guarantees: off-budget until called, then debt**. In India CSR is a statutory obligation for qualifying companies under the Companies Act, which separates it from voluntary corporate philanthropy elsewhere.
notes.71: INGOs deliver, channel money and advocate, and critics ask why Northern organisations still capture funding meant for Southern communities. The critique has produced concrete commitments partly because it came from inside the sector. The defence is that INGOs absorb compliance risk, and the slide calls that **a problem to solve**.
notes.72: Multipolarity gives recipients more funders, bargaining power and alternatives, at the cost of more reporting regimes and weaker collective standards. The slide's final point: **choice is only valuable to a state with the capacity to use it**. A strong finance ministry gains, while a weak one facing thirty uncoordinated funders has a governance problem.
notes.74: Quality matters as much as quantity. Many small projects, parallel donor systems, donor-driven priorities and volatile disbursement burden the ministries meant to deliver. The slide calls **volatility** the most damaging: a government cannot put teachers or nurses on the payroll against funding that may not arrive next year.
notes.75: Memorise the five Paris principles: ownership, alignment, harmonisation, results and mutual accountability. Reviews found that recipient-side commitments moved faster than donor-side ones. **Alignment is hardest**, since it asks a donor to accept audit risk in another state's systems, a decision for the donor's audit office and parliament.
notes.76: Read the sequence as a trade-off: Paris 2005, Accra 2008, Busan 2011 and the Grand Bargain in 2016. Busan brought in non-DAC providers on voluntary terms, which is **why they came and why the regime weakened**. The choice is a binding agreement among a small club or a voluntary one that includes everyone who matters.
notes.77: Ownership is the most important principle and the hardest to honour. The table pairs each requirement with what it collides with: earmarking, fiduciary rules, budget cycles and results frameworks. The slide's verdict: ownership is usually real **where the government had the capacity and weight to insist**.
notes.78: Localisation moves funding, decision-making and leadership to local organisations. The table shows what blocks each. The sharpest is **risk**: local partners take on delivery in hard settings while liability stays with the international partner. Direct funding percentages are the weakest headline metric, since money passed through on the same conditions transfers no decision-making.
notes.79: The Grand Bargain of 2016 committed donors to channel funding as directly as possible to local responders. The chart is illustrative. Progress has been slow, and the hardest part is **defining and measuring 'direct'**. Several commitments cut against donors' own domestic incentives, and the annual reporting has been frank.
notes.80: Decolonising aid goes beyond logistics: it questions **whose knowledge counts**, who leads, which language sets the terms and who is treated as expert and who as beneficiary. It differs from localisation, which concerns funds and authority. The slide warns it is the agenda most easily absorbed as vocabulary.
notes.81: Obstacles hold because of incentives: donors answer to their auditors, compliance rules favour large intermediaries and those with the money set the criteria. Treat 'capacity' with suspicion. Apply the slide's test: what would **count as sufficient capacity, who assesses it and on what timetable**?
notes.83: The aid-works, aid-harms and aid-is-marginal positions are less contradictory than they look, because they describe **different things**: specific interventions, political incentives and aggregate growth. The slide's reading of the literature: aid works well where the outcome is technical and measurable, and badly where it substitutes for a political settlement.
notes.84: The dependency argument has conditions. Where aid is a small share of the budget the accountability argument is weak, and where it funds most public spending it is strong. Note the concrete last row: **donor-funded organisations pay above public-sector rates**, drawing skilled staff out of ministries.
notes.85: Dead Aid argued that aid to African governments encouraged dependency, and critics reply that targeted aid has saved lives. The slide stresses that the book targeted **government-to-government aid** and left humanitarian and health assistance aside, a distinction often lost. Read it beside Sachs and Easterly for the full range of the argument.
notes.86: Paternalism means outside experts deciding for communities. The alternatives in the table are co-design with a real veto, decision-makers in place of beneficiaries, and asking and acting on the answer. **Consultation without authority** is the common failure: if the answer cannot change the programme, participants see it as legitimation.
notes.87: Conditionality raises a sovereignty question: who sets the budget, decides what is public, legislates and bears the political cost? Subsidy removal makes it most visible, because the government carries the unrest for a condition it did not choose. The formal defence, that governments can decline the loan, **depends on there being an alternative**.
notes.88: Power runs through measurement: which outcomes count, whose indicators, which language and which methodology. The practical example is proposal format. A funding round that requires a **theory of change in a particular format** selects for organisations with someone able to write one, whatever the quality of their work.
notes.89: Upward accountability to donors is contractual, resourced and enforced, while downward accountability to communities rests on goodwill and is rarely resourced. The slide says the **asymmetry is no oversight**, because only upward accountability has a legal instrument behind it. Where downward accountability worked, it was given teeth, such as an independent grievance decision-maker.
notes.90: End with the balanced view: aid has saved lives and it has also distorted incentives and entrenched power. Hold both. The most useful stance is specific: **this instrument, in this country, with these terms**, is or is not doing what it claims. A practitioner who believes only the critique cannot work inside the system.
notes.92: India's position has flipped: from among the largest aid recipients to a provider of cooperation, while it still borrows from the World Bank and ADB. The 1991 IMF programme is the pivot in domestic memory, so **conditionality is remembered from the receiving end**. Use the four steps to describe India as both recipient and giver.
notes.93: India's cooperation runs through the MEA and its Development Partnership Administration, using lines of credit, grants, training (ITEC) and humanitarian assistance. **Lines of credit dominate by value and are concessional loans**, so most Indian cooperation is debt. It concentrates on the neighbourhood and Africa.
notes.94: Apply the course's consistency test: India frames its cooperation as South–South partnership with no policy conditionality, yet contracts often specify Indian sourcing. The slide says sourcing is how lines of credit are structured, and it is **tied aid by the standard definition**. Hold India to the same standard as DAC donors.
notes.95: India's 2023 G20 presidency pushed debt, climate finance and digital public infrastructure, and secured permanent membership for the African Union. The slide separates the concrete outcome from agenda-setting: **the African Union's admission is agreed and the rest is incremental**. Its test for a presidency is what it agreed, a shorter list than what it proposed.
notes.96: India pushes for a Security Council seat, a bigger IMF quota and World Bank voting realignment. Each demand meets the same structural fact: **the bodies that must approve change are governed by the states that would lose from it**. The Global South votes as a bloc rarely, and coalitions form issue by issue.
notes.97: Read the tensions in the table as analysis. India champions the South abroad while hosting a large share of global poverty, seeks IFI voting reform while borrowing from them, and frames aid as unconditional while structuring credit with sourcing conditions. The lesson: **international framing and domestic record are separate evidence**.
notes.98: This reading list gives you the full range of the aid debate: Moyo's critique, Sachs's case for big aid, Easterly's sceptic reply and Banerjee and Duflo's evidence-first approach. Pair it with the OECD-DAC, UN SDG and World Bank portals for the numbers. Read **at least two authors who disagree**.
notes.99: The five takeaways are your revision list. The habit worth keeping is three questions for any development figure: **who counted it, under whose definition, and is it a gift or a loan**. The slide says they resolve most confusion without specialist knowledge of the institution. The table repeats each section's single message.
